lead: This unit gives the two systematic ways to solve any circuit, mesh currents and node voltages, and the network theorems that replace a complicated network by a simple one. After it you can solve DC and AC circuits with independent and dependent sources, find Thevenin and Norton equivalents, choose the load for maximum power, and predict the effect of changing one element.
about: The first two chapters turn Kirchhoff's laws into methods: mesh analysis writes KVL with mesh currents and handles current sources with a supermesh; nodal analysis writes KCL with node voltages and handles voltage sources with a supernode. Linearity and superposition explain why a circuit can be solved one source at a time, and that idea proves the rest. Thevenin's and Norton's theorems shrink any two-terminal network to two numbers, which the maximum power transfer theorem then uses to pick the best load. Reciprocity, Millman's and Tellegen's theorems add shortcuts and a power-balance check, and the compensation theorem finds what happens when one element changes. The last chapter carries every method and theorem over to AC circuits with phasors and impedances, ending with the conjugate match.

chapters.idea: Mesh currents turn KVL round every window into a small set of linear equations; a current source on a shared branch becomes one supermesh equation plus one constraint.
Node voltages turn KCL at every non-reference node into a small set of linear equations; a voltage source between two nodes becomes one supernode equation plus one constraint.
In a linear circuit the response to several sources is the sum of the responses to each independent source alone, with the others switched off and dependent sources kept.
Any linear two-terminal network equals V<sub>th</sub> in series with R<sub>th</sub>, or I<sub>N</sub> in parallel with R<sub>N</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>.
A fixed network gives a load the most power when R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>; that power is V<sub>th</sub>²/(4R<sub>th</sub>) at no better than 50 % efficiency.
Reciprocity swaps source and response, Millman collapses parallel source branches, and Tellegen's theorem says branch powers add to zero.
A change ΔZ in a branch carrying I changes every current by what a source IΔZ, acting alone, drives through the changed network.
With phasors and impedances every DC method and theorem holds at one frequency; maximum power needs the conjugate match.
